title: The Two Worlds and the River: Calw, Maulbronn, Ceylon, and forty-three years on the Collina d'Oro
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Calw, the birth on the Marktplatz
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinate corrected to the Marktplatz (Nominatim, Marktplatz 30); the point in circulation, 48.7169, 8.7332, is some 380 m off the square.
stops.campa: On the second of July a son is born at Marktplatz 6 in Calw, a Black Forest town on the Nagold, to Johannes Hesse, a Baltic German missionary turned publisher for the mission press, and to Marie Gundert, born in India to the missionary and Malayalam lexicographer Hermann Gundert. The house stands on the market square of a Württemberg town of clockmakers and tanners. The child is a Russian subject through his father, in a German empire six years old, in a family whose real country is a mission field in south India none of them can quite leave alone.
suggested_refs: The birth house at Marktplatz 6, Calw, now part of the Hermann-Hesse-Museum quarter

stops.name: Basel, the house of the mission
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month unknown, defaulted to January. Coordinate corrected 1.2 km to the Basel Mission compound at Missionsstrasse 21 in Grossbasel; the point in circulation falls in Kleinbasel, across the Rhine.
stops.campa: Johannes Hesse is called to Basel to edit the mission's magazine, and the family crosses into Switzerland when the boy is four. They live in the orbit of the compound on the Missionsstrasse: archives, returning missionaries, the objects and languages of India and West Africa arriving in crates from men his grandfather trained. Six years here make the child fluent in two Germanies, the Swabian and the Swiss. He will come back to this city as a bookseller's apprentice at twenty-two, and to this country as a citizen at forty-six.
suggested_refs: The Basel Mission archive at Missionsstrasse 21, mission 21

stops.name: Calw, the return and the Latin school
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing: the UCSB Hesse Chronology dates the return 1886, English Wikipedia 1887. Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: The family comes back to Calw and the boy enters the Reallyzeum, the town's Latin school. The house he grows up in holds two worlds that do not touch: the lit one of hymns, lamplight, and missionary discipline, and the dark one of the street, the servants, the river, and everything unpermitted. He moves between them all day and belongs to neither. Thirty-three years later he will hand both worlds to a boy called Emil Sinclair, publish the book under Sinclair's name, and let a generation of demobilized German soldiers recognise their own childhoods in it.
stops.quote: And the oddest thing was, how closely the two worlds bordered each other, how near they both were!
stops.quote_source: Demian, English translation (New York: Boni & Liveright, 1923; Project Gutenberg ebook #74222, translator not credited)
suggested_refs: The Reallyzeum of Calw, the town's Latin school

stops.name: Göppingen, the Latin school and the state examination
stops.date_confidence: the year at Göppingen is attested by the UCSB chronology; no month is given, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He is sent away to the Latin school at Göppingen for a year, to be drilled for the Württemberg state examination that admits boys to the church seminaries. It is the funnel of the Swabian Protestant elite: Latin, Greek, and a free education paid for with a life pledged to the church. He passes it. His parents, who gave their own lives to the Basel Mission, deliver the thirteen-year-old to the machine that made them. The machine takes him in the September of the following year.
suggested_refs: The Württemberg Landexamen, the state entrance examination for the church seminaries

stops.name: Maulbronn, the seminary and the flight
stops.date_confidence: 1891 attested; the day 15 September that circulates is unsupported by either Wikipedia, so the stop is dated to the month. The flight is attested for March 1892; the UCSB chronology gives 7 March, English Wikipedia only the month. Coordinate corrected ~900 m to the abbey itself.
stops.campa: At fourteen he enters the Evangelical Theological Seminary housed in the Cistercian abbey of Maulbronn, a walled monastery turned boarding school. He lasts about six months. In March he walks out through the gate and is found the next day lying in a field, and from that moment the machinery of correction closes on him: retrieval, punishment, and the finding that the boy is not disobedient but ill. He will write the school again in Unterm Rad as Hans Giebenrath's, and in the book he will let the boy die of it.
stops.quote: The bird fights its way out of the egg. The egg is the world. Whoever will be born must destroy a world. The bird flies to God. The name of the god is Abraxas.
stops.quote_source: Demian, English translation (New York: Boni & Liveright, 1923; Project Gutenberg ebook #74222)
suggested_refs: Kloster Maulbronn, the Evangelisch-theologisches Seminar

stops.name: Bad Boll, under Blumhardt
stops.date_confidence: May 1892 per both Wikipedias; the geography source in the pool says June, contradicting the chronology in the same pool. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected 2.6 km north to Bad Boll proper.
stops.campa: He is delivered to Christoph Friedrich Blumhardt at Bad Boll, a pietist theologian celebrated for healing by prayer and for casting out spirits, on the theory that what ails the boy is spiritual. It does not hold. He attempts to kill himself, and Blumhardt sends him on to the nerve clinic at Stetten im Remstal, where he is kept among patients far sicker than he is. He is fourteen. In one year he has been handed to a seminary, a faith healer, and an asylum, and none of the three has any idea what he is.
suggested_refs: The Blumhardt institution at Bad Boll; the Nervenheilanstalt at Stetten im Remstal

stops.name: Bad Cannstatt, the Gymnasium and the One Year Examination
stops.date_confidence: the placement at Cannstatt at the end of 1892 is attested; the month is inferred from the sequence Stetten, Basel, Cannstatt. The examination itself is attested for 1893.
stops.campa: After Stetten and a boys' institution in Basel he is put into the Gymnasium at Bad Cannstatt outside Stuttgart, the fourth institution inside a single year. He passes the One Year Examination in 1893, the certificate that ends compulsory schooling, and that is the whole of the formal education of the man to whom Stockholm will give the Nobel Prize in Literature fifty-three years later. Everything he knows after this he takes out of bookshops, which is where he spends the next decade.
suggested_refs: The Einjährigen-Examen, the Württemberg one-year certificate

stops.name: Calw, the Perrot tower-clock factory
stops.date_confidence: 1894 attested for the start of the fourteen-month apprenticeship; the month is inferred backward from the attested move to Tübingen in October 1895. The factory site inside Calw was not pinpointed, so the town-centre coordinate stands as an approximation.
stops.campa: A bookseller's apprenticeship at Esslingen am Neckar collapses within days, and he comes home to Calw with no trade and no school. His father puts him into the Perrot tower-clock works as a mechanic's apprentice, and for fourteen months he files and fits gear trains for clocks that will be hoisted into church towers across Württemberg. It is the only manual trade he ever learns. He is seventeen, and the works turn out clocks by catalogue for parishes he will never see.
suggested_refs: The Perrot Turmuhrenfabrik of Calw, tower-clock makers

stops.name: Tübingen, Heckenhauer and the first books
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by hermann-hesse.de and the UCSB chronology.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of October he begins at the Heckenhauer bookshop in Tübingen: three years as an apprentice, then a year as an assistant, long days among theology and philology stock in a university town. He reads Goethe and the Romantics at night, on his own account, with no teacher. In 1896 a poem called Madonna is printed and the collection Romantische Lieder follows; in 1898 Eugen Diederichs brings out the prose of Eine Stunde hinter Mitternacht. Neither sells. He is a published author and a shop assistant at the same counter.
suggested_refs: The Heckenhauer Buchhandlung, Tübingen, still trading

stops.name: Basel, the Reich bookshop
stops.date_confidence: autumn 1899 attested; day unknown, defaulted to 01. The chronology that calls this post antiquarian is wrong by two years: this is the ordinary Reich'sche Buchhandlung, and the Antiquariat Wattenwyl comes in August 1901.
stops.campa: In the autumn he moves to Basel and the Reich'sche Buchhandlung, an ordinary bookshop selling new books, and re-enters as a young professional the city he left as a boy of ten. The following year the army examines him and rejects him for an eye condition, the first of the times a defective body will keep him out of a uniform. He is twenty-two, minimally schooled, unmarried, in print, and unread. The mission house is a walk away; his grandfather's Malayalam dictionary is in the archive there, and India is still only a room in a family building.
suggested_refs: The Reich'sche Buchhandlung, Basel

stops.name: Florence, the Piazza del Duomo
stops.date_confidence: the journey is attested for March to May 1901 and the stop list is attested; the individual dates are ordered reconstruction inside that window, not documented.
stops.campa: His first Italian journey runs from March to May, out of Basel through Milan and the port of Genoa and down into Tuscany. In Florence he walks the Duomo and the galleries with the guidebook of a bookseller who has sold a hundred Baedekers and never used one. He travels alone, on a shop assistant's savings, sleeping cheap. Italy gives him what it gave German travellers for a century before him: a south, and a Christianity that is not Swabian pietism. He will spend the next three years writing out of it.
suggested_refs: The Piazza del Duomo and the Uffizi, Florence, on the 1901 itinerary

stops.name: Ravenna, the mosaics of San Vitale
stops.date_confidence: Ravenna is attested on the 1901 itinerary; the date is ordered reconstruction inside the attested March to May window.
stops.campa: At Ravenna he stands in San Vitale under gold Byzantine tesserae, Justinian and Theodora facing each other across the apse in a Christian art that is neither Gothic, nor northern, nor pietist, nor even quite European. It is the first religion he has seen that is made out of colour rather than out of argument. He has been raised on hymnbooks and mission reports; twenty years stand between this apse and the Indian and Chinese material he will spend the rest of his life inside.
suggested_refs: The Basilica di San Vitale, Ravenna, and its sixth-century mosaics

stops.name: Venice, the Piazza San Marco
stops.date_confidence: Venice is attested as the closing stop of the 1901 journey; the date is ordered reconstruction inside the attested window.
stops.campa: The journey closes in Venice, in the Piazza San Marco, the city that stands in the German imagination for Italy entire. He is twenty-three and famous nowhere. Eleven years from now Thomas Mann will send Gustav von Aschenbach to die on this lagoon; Hesse simply looks, writes it down, and takes the train north to a bookshop job. The Italy of 1901 gives him the setting of his first successful book, and the taste for the south that will end, eighteen years later, in a Swiss canton where the language is Italian.
suggested_refs: The Piazza San Marco, Venice, terminus of the 1901 journey

stops.name: Basel, the Antiquariat Wattenwyl and Peter Camenzind
stops.date_confidence: August 1901 per de.wikipedia; the April 1901 date in circulation is wrong and would also collide with the Italian journey. Peter Camenzind and the marriage are attested for 1904.
stops.campa: In August he moves to the Antiquariat Wattenwyl, dealing in old books instead of new ones. Three years later Samuel Fischer publishes Peter Camenzind, a peasant boy who goes to the city and comes home again, and the book sells; Sigmund Freud will praise it. At twenty-seven Hesse stops being a shop assistant who writes and becomes a writer who does nothing else. In the same year he marries Maria Bernoulli, photographer, nine years older than he is, of the Basel family of mathematicians, while her father is out of the country.
suggested_refs: The Antiquariat Wattenwyl, Basel; the first edition of Peter Camenzind, S. Fischer, 1904

stops.name: Gaienhofen, the marriage and the rented farmhouse
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by hermann-hesse.de and de.wikipedia. Coordinate corrected 1.2 km southwest to the village; the point in circulation falls out in the lake.
stops.campa: On the tenth of August the couple settle at Gaienhofen, a village on the German shore of the Bodensee with no railway and no shop worth the name. They rent a farmhouse. He writes, gardens, and rows on the lake; Maria plays Chopin in the evening. Bruno is born in 1905. Unterm Rad appears in 1906, the seminary book, the revenge taken on Maulbronn fourteen years after the field. The marriage that begins here as a retreat from the world will finish as a confinement inside it, and he will write that book too.
suggested_refs: The rented farmhouse at Gaienhofen, 1904 to 1907

stops.name: Ascona, the mountain of truth
stops.date_confidence: April 1907 attested by de.wikipedia; day unknown, defaulted to 01. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from the corpus pin for Monte Verità in laban.journey.json, so that the hill is one point on the atlas.
stops.campa: Taking a cure at Locarno in April, he climbs to Monte Verità above Ascona, where vegetarians, nudists, theosophists, anarchists, and sun-worshippers are attempting to resign from the nineteenth century by living in huts on a hill. He looks, and does not stay. The doctrines mean nothing to him. What he keeps is the premise underneath them: a man may leave his civilization on his own authority. Six years later Rudolf von Laban will bring his dancers up the same slope. Ticino sees Hesse here for the first time, twelve years before it keeps him.
suggested_refs: The Lebensreform colony of Monte Verità above Ascona

stops.name: Gaienhofen, the built house and the three sons
stops.date_confidence: the built house is attested from 1907, Heiner's birth for 1909, Martin's for 1911; the stop is dated to the middle year, month defaulted to January.
stops.campa: From 1907 the family lives in a house built to their own order, and by 1911 there are three sons in it: Bruno, Heiner, Martin. Hesse is the successful author of the German provinces, admired for lakes and forests and the small clean life, invited to lecture on it. He is also, by his own account afterwards, suffocating. Gertrud appears in 1910 and he calls it a miscarriage. Rosshalde, written next, is about a painter who cannot leave a marriage or a house. He writes the diagnosis three years before he acts on it.
suggested_refs: The Hesse house at Gaienhofen, built 1907

stops.name: Genoa, boarding the Prinz Eitel Friedrich
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The ship's name and the 6 September departure rest on a single secondary source, straitsindie.substack.com, and are corroborated by neither Wikipedia. The voyage itself is attested for autumn 1911.
stops.campa: On the sixth of September he boards a steamer at Genoa with the painter Hans Sturzenegger and sails east. He has been reading Indian scripture since he could read; his mother was born in India, his grandfather compiled a Malayalam dictionary there, and the crates in the Basel mission house came from there. He is going to find the India of the family library. He will not find it. The route runs Suez, Penang, Malaya, Singapore, Sumatra, Ceylon, and never touches the subcontinent that is the entire reason for the voyage.
suggested_refs: The Norddeutscher Lloyd steamer Prinz Eitel Friedrich on the Genoa to Far East run

stops.name: Penang, the harbour of George Town
stops.date_confidence: 27 September 1911 per straitsindie.substack.com, a single secondary source; not contradicted by anything reachable.
stops.campa: The steamer comes into Penang on the twenty-seventh of September and Sturzenegger's brother Robert, a planter, meets them on the quay. This is the Asia that actually exists: British harbour law, Chinese shophouses, Tamil labour, rubber and tin, and Europeans running the whole apparatus at a profit. Hesse walks it as a tourist carrying letters of introduction. The disappointment that runs through the rest of the voyage starts here, in the distance between the Orient of Schopenhauer and his grandfather's shelves and the colonial Malaya of 1911.
suggested_refs: George Town harbour, Penang, Straits Settlements

stops.name: Singapore, the hinge of the voyage
stops.date_confidence: October 1911 attested for the Singapore leg; the day is reconstruction inside the month.
stops.campa: Singapore is the pivot of the itinerary: from this harbour he goes on to Sumatra, and back to it before the passage home. He has crossed the peninsula overland first, through the tin towns of Ipoh and Kuala Lumpur and the Sultan's palace at Johor. What he sets down is heat, dirt, commerce, and his own irritation with himself for expecting otherwise. The pilgrim's Asia refuses to appear anywhere on the route. A modern English selection of these pieces is titled Singapore Dream, which is nearer the truth than the traveller was.
suggested_refs: Singapore harbour, 1911; the travel pieces collected as Singapore Dream and Other Adventures

stops.name: Kuching, the disputed Borneo leg
stops.date_confidence: unverified tradition. The Borneo leg rests on a publisher's book description retrieved through search; de.wikipedia's itinerary omits it entirely. The coordinate in circulation is kept as it stands but reverse-geocodes to Kuching in Sarawak, which is not the Dutch East Indies the summary claims.
stops.campa: Between Singapore and Sumatra the tradition puts him briefly ashore on Borneo. The point that circulates for it falls at Kuching in Sarawak, the private kingdom the Brooke rajahs have held for seventy years, a white raj of river forts, Chinese gold miners, and a headhunting frontier under British protection. If he went, he wrote almost nothing about it. Ceylon fills a book; Borneo leaves one line in a publisher's summary, no landscape and no date anybody can check.
suggested_refs: The Raj of Sarawak under the Brooke rajahs, 1911
sources: Goodreads and Shambhala descriptions of 'Singapore Dream and Other Adventures', via search

stops.name: Medan, the sickness in the plantation country
stops.date_confidence: October 1911 attested for the Sumatra leg; the day is reconstruction inside the month.
stops.campa: He goes ashore in Sumatra, in the Dutch plantation country behind Belawan, and there his stomach gives out. The illness cancels the passage to southern India, the thing he came for. Everything after this is a retreat. He has crossed half the world to be defeated by food and water. The India of Hermann Gundert's lexicon and Marie Hesse's birth stays over the horizon for the rest of his life, and he will write Siddhartha eleven years later without having stood in the country once.
suggested_refs: The Deli plantation country behind Belawan and Medan, Dutch East Indies

stops.name: Colombo, the landfall in Ceylon
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing. The geography source dates the Colombo landfall to September 1911, but the route it gives for the same voyage runs Genoa, Suez, Penang, Malaya, Singapore, Sumatra, Ceylon, which puts Ceylon last and cannot hold with a 27 September arrival at Penang. The route order is followed here; the September dating is recorded and not resolved.
stops.campa: Ceylon is the last of it and the best. He lands at Colombo, the port that opens the island, and for the first time in three months he is somewhere that answers him rather than sells to him. The book he makes of the journey is called Aus Indien, From India, and it takes its title from a country he never set foot in and its substance from this island and from Malaya. He will do it again with Siddhartha: the name on the map stays Indian and the ground under it is this island and a Swiss hill.
suggested_refs: Aus Indien (1913), the book made from the 1911 voyage

stops.name: Kandy, the Temple of the Tooth
stops.date_confidence: the Kandy visit is attested; the date follows the reconstructed Ceylon leg and inherits its uncertainty. Burma, which appears on the English-language itinerary, is dropped: de.wikipedia states flatly that he was never in India and lists only Ceylon and Indonesia.
stops.campa: He goes up from Colombo into the hills to Kandy and the Sri Dalada Maligawa, where a tooth of the Buddha is kept behind gold and guarded by drummers. This is Buddhism as a living cult of monks, pilgrims, flowers, and noise, not the philosophical Buddhism of the German translations he was raised on. He climbs higher, toward Pidurutalagala above the tea country, the island's highest mountain. Everything in Siddhartha that is neither Indian scripture nor Swabian pietism comes out of these weeks on this island.
stops.quote: Beliefs are not important, they can be beautiful or ugly, clever or foolish, anyone can stay attached to them or throw them away.
stops.quote_source: Siddhartha, chapter 'Gotama,' trans. David Wyllie (Project Gutenberg ebook #58344, from the 1922 German)
suggested_refs: The Sri Dalada Maligawa, Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, Kandy

stops.name: Bern, Melchenbühlweg 26
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia gives late summer 1912, Spätsommer, and the address; day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinate corrected 1.5 km northeast to the Melchenbühlweg itself.
stops.campa: In late summer the family leaves the Bodensee for Bern and an old house on the edge of the city at Melchenbühlweg 26. Hesse is thirty-five and has left Germany, as it turns out, permanently: he will never live in it again. Maria keeps the household, he keeps a study, and the house repairs nothing. Rosshalde comes out in 1914, a novel about an artist whose home has become a cage and whose child dies, and it is published in the year that everything he has been writing privately becomes a public catastrophe.
suggested_refs: The house at Melchenbühlweg 26, Bern

stops.name: Bern, O Friends, Not These Tones
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the essay appears in the Neue Zürcher Zeitung on 3 November 1914.
stops.campa: He volunteers for the Imperial Army in August and is found unfit to fight, and the book service for German prisoners of war takes him instead; it will hold him until 1919. On the third of November the Neue Zürcher Zeitung prints his essay O Freunde, nicht diese Töne, taking Schiller's line out of the Ninth Symphony and turning it against the war fever of the German intellectuals. He asks writers not to poison the future with hatred. The German press answers by calling him a traitor and a shirker. Publishers drop him. The hate mail runs for years.
suggested_refs: O Freunde, nicht diese Töne, Neue Zürcher Zeitung, 3 November 1914; the Bücherzentrale für deutsche Kriegsgefangene, Bern

stops.name: Lucerne, the analysis
stops.date_confidence: 1916 attested for the treatment near Lucerne with a Jungian analyst; the month is inferred and the analyst's name, Josef Bernhard Lang, is carried from outside the verified pool as reconstruction. The father's death is attested for March 1916 by English Wikipedia, for the year only by the UCSB chronology.
stops.campa: His father dies in March, his son Martin falls dangerously ill, and Maria's schizophrenia breaks open. Hesse leaves the prisoner-of-war service and goes into treatment near Lucerne with a pupil of Carl Gustav Jung, some seventy sessions across the worst year of the war. The analyst gives him shadow, anima, and individuation as working words, and Hesse gives the analyst back, transfigured, as the organist Pistorius in Demian. The Zurich school enters German literature here, in a sanatorium, through a writer his own country has stopped printing.
stops.quote: When we hate a man, we hate in him something which resides in us ourselves. What is not in us does not move us.
stops.quote_source: Demian, chapter six, 'Jacob Wrestles with God,' spoken by Pistorius; English translation (New York: Boni & Liveright, 1923; Project Gutenberg ebook #74222)
suggested_refs: The Sonnmatt sanatorium near Lucerne; the analytical practice of Josef Bernhard Lang

stops.name: Bern, Demian in six weeks
stops.date_confidence: September to October 1917 attested for the writing; the stop is dated to the start of that span. Publication under the name Emil Sinclair is attested for 1919.
stops.campa: In September and October, in about six weeks, he writes Demian: The Story of Emil Sinclair's Youth. It is published in 1919 over Sinclair's name, and the disguise holds long enough for the book to be given the Fontane Prize for a first novel, which Hesse then has to hand back. A generation of German soldiers coming home out of the trenches reads it as though it had been written about them personally. Thomas Mann will say its effect was the effect of Werther. Hesse is forty and has begun again under another man's name.
stops.quote: I wanted only to try to live in obedience to the promptings which came from my true self. Why was that so very difficult?
stops.quote_source: Demian: The Story of Emil Sinclair's Youth, epigraph; English translation (New York: Boni & Liveright, 1923; Project Gutenberg ebook #74222)
suggested_refs: The first edition of Demian, S. Fischer, 1919, under the pseudonym Emil Sinclair

stops.name: Minusio, the arrival in Ticino
stops.date_confidence: the chronology in circulation attaches 25 April 1919 to Minusio, which the sources do not allow. de.wikipedia has him moving to Ticino in mid-April and to Sorengo on 25 April; en.wikipedia has him at Sorengo from 25 April to 11 May. The stop is dated mid-April and the misjoined variant is recorded here.
stops.campa: In the middle of April he crosses the Alps alone into the Italian canton, leaving Maria in a clinic and the three boys placed with friends. He takes first a small farmhouse at the entrance to Minusio above Lake Maggiore, then rooms at Sorengo for a fortnight. He is forty-one. He has no household, almost no income, and no country that will print him. He has come back to the region he first saw from Monte Verità in 1907. What starts here is the most productive decade of his life and the loneliest.
suggested_refs: The farmhouse at the entrance to Minusio; the lodging at Sorengo, 25 April to 11 May 1919

stops.name: Montagnola, the Casa Camuzzi
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from the corpus pin for Montagnola in serrano.journey.json; Nominatim would put the village at 45.9830, 8.9184, and a future re-pinning should move Hesse and Serrano together.
stops.campa: On the eleventh of May he moves into four rooms of the Casa Camuzzi at Montagnola on the Collina d'Oro, a Ticinese architect's fantasy of a baroque hunting lodge above Lugano. He lives on nearly nothing, in one suit, and starts painting watercolours because words have stopped being sufficient. Klingsors letzter Sommer comes out of the first summer, a painter burning himself away in a southern landscape. In these four rooms, over the next three years, he writes Siddhartha.
stops.quote: “This is a beautiful river,” he said to his companion. “Yes,” said the ferry man, “it is a very beautiful river, I love it above all else. I have many times listened to what it has to say, many times looked into its eyes, and it has always had something to teach me. There is a great deal that you can learn from a river.”
stops.quote_source: Siddhartha, chapter 'Kamala,' trans. David Wyllie (Project Gutenberg ebook #58344), lines 1221-1226
suggested_refs: The Casa Camuzzi, Montagnola, and the watercolours begun there in 1919

stops.name: Montagnola, Siddhartha
stops.date_confidence: 1922 attested for publication; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Siddhartha is published: a Brahmin's son who walks away from the ascetics, from the Buddha, from the merchant and the courtesan, and gets what he needs from a ferryman and a river. Hesse writes it having never reached India, out of his grandfather's lexicon, his mother's birthplace, three weeks in Ceylon, and eighteen months in the middle when the book would not go on at all. In the same years Hermann Keyserling runs his School of Wisdom at Darmstadt and brings Tagore to Germany. Postwar Europe is ransacking Asia for a way to live.
stops.quote: What I wanted to learn was my self, I wanted to learn the meaning and the essence of my self. I wanted to be rid of my self, wanted to overcome my self.
stops.quote_source: Siddhartha, chapter 'Awakening,' trans. David Wyllie (Project Gutenberg ebook #58344)
suggested_refs: The first edition of Siddhartha, S. Fischer, 1922

stops.name: Montagnola, the Swiss passport and the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: citizenship and the dissolution of the first marriage attested for 1923, the marriage to Ruth Wenger for 1924, Kurgast for 1925; months unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: In 1923 the marriage to Maria is formally dissolved and Hesse takes Swiss citizenship, ending the German nationality he was raised into in Württemberg. In 1924 he marries Ruth Wenger, a singer half his age, daughter of the writer Lisa Wenger. They barely manage to live in the same house. He spends the winters at Baden taking the waters for sciatica and writes Kurgast about it, a book by a man observing his own body and his own bad temper with the attention he once gave to lakes.
stops.quote: You can beg for love, buy love, receive love as a gift, you can find it on the street, but you cannot steal love.
stops.quote_source: Siddhartha, chapter 'Kamala,' spoken by Kamala; trans. David Wyllie (Project Gutenberg ebook #58344)
suggested_refs: Kurgast (1925), the Baden sanatorium narrative

stops.name: Montagnola, Steppenwolf
stops.date_confidence: the divorce from Ruth Wenger, Die Nürnberger Reise and Der Steppenwolf are all attested for 1927; months unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The claim that cohabitation with Ninon began this year is dropped as unsettled.
stops.campa: He is fifty. The marriage to Ruth is dissolved; Die Nürnberger Reise and Der Steppenwolf are published in the same twelve months. Steppenwolf is the book of a man locked into rented rooms with a razor and a gramophone, split between a bourgeois who wants order and a wolf that wants to tear the order apart, and offered instead a jazz band, a woman, a drug, and a Magic Theater. Hugo Ball, his neighbour on this hill and the first man to write his life, dies at Sant'Abbondio in September.
stops.quote: Man and wolf would then be compelled to recognise one another without the masks of false feeling and to look one another straight in the eye.
stops.quote_source: Steppenwolf, 'Treatise on the Steppenwolf,' trans. Basil Creighton (1929), revised by Joseph Mileck and Horst Frenz
suggested_refs: Hugo Ball, Hermann Hesse: sein Leben und sein Werk (1927)

stops.name: Arosa, the winters with Ninon
stops.date_confidence: de.wikipedia supports extended winter holidays at Arosa in 1928 and 1929 only; the 1925 date and the framing as the mid-1920s that circulate are unsupported. When cohabitation with Ninon began is not settled: English Wikipedia implies 1930, German Wikipedia gives no year at all.
stops.campa: He spends the winters of 1928 and 1929 at Arosa in the Grisons, high in the snow, with Ninon Dolbin, born Ausländer, an art historian a good deal younger than he is. She will organise the rest of his life: the correspondence, the household, the defences against visitors and admirers. Narziss und Goldmund appears in 1930, the friendship of a monk who stays and a wanderer who goes, the two halves of a nature he has been trying for thirty years to get into one man and has never managed.
suggested_refs: The Arosa winters of 1928 and 1929; Narziss und Goldmund (1930)

stops.name: Montagnola, the Casa Rossa
stops.date_confidence: the marriage to Ninon on 14 November 1931 and the move to the Bodmer house are attested. The coordinate is the one in circulation for the Casa Rossa and has not been independently geocoded; it is a distinct building from the Casa Camuzzi and is deliberately not given the inherited Montagnola pin.
stops.campa: His patron Hans C. Bodmer builds him a house above Montagnola and gives him the use of it for life. On the fourteenth of November he marries Ninon and they move in. He is fifty-four and has a permanent address for the first time since Gaienhofen. He will live here thirty-one years and finish one book. Die Morgenlandfahrt appears in 1932, a short account of a pilgrimage eastward made by a league of travellers drawn out of every century at once, and it is the study for the work that takes the next eleven years.
suggested_refs: The Casa Rossa above Montagnola, built for Hesse by Hans C. Bodmer

stops.name: Montagnola, The Glass Bead Game
stops.date_confidence: 1943 attested for publication in Switzerland after German refusal; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. The exile assistance and the reviews of banned authors are attested for 1933 onward.
stops.campa: Das Glasperlenspiel is published in Zurich, German houses having refused it under Nazi pressure. It is set centuries ahead in Castalia, a province of scholars who play one game that unites music, mathematics, and all the sciences, and whose Magister Ludi finally walks out of the province altogether. Through the thirties Hesse has helped Thomas Mann and Bertolt Brecht into exile and reviewed banned Jewish authors, Kafka among them, and has been attacked from both directions: too Jewish for Berlin, too soft on Germany for the exiles.
suggested_refs: Das Glasperlenspiel, Fretz und Wasmuth, Zurich, 1943

stops.name: Stockholm, the empty chair at the Konserthuset
stops.date_confidence: attested: announced 14 November 1946, ceremony 10 December 1946, non-attendance and the acceptance by the Swiss envoy confirmed by en.wikipedia's article on the 1946 prize. The coordinate is the Konserthuset, the ceremony site; the point in circulation for this event falls in Gamla stan and is mislabelled Swedish Academy. The prize was not shared: nobelprize.org gives a prize share of 1/1.
stops.campa: On the tenth of December the Nobel Prize in Literature is presented at the Stockholm Konserthuset. Hesse is not in the hall. His health keeps him at Montagnola and the envoy of the Swiss republic accepts on his behalf, a Swiss laureate for a Swabian who left Germany in 1912 and gave up its nationality in 1923. Frankfurt gives him the Goethe Prize the same year. He is sixty-nine, his books have been burned or refused in the country of his language, and the world has decided, at this exact moment, to make him a classic.
stops.quote: for his inspired writings which, while growing in boldness and penetration, exemplify the classical humanitarian ideals and high qualities of style
stops.quote_source: Nobel Prize in Literature 1946, official motivation, nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/1946/summary/

stops.name: Montagnola, Miguel Serrano at the table
stops.date_confidence: the date is carried from serrano.journey.json, where the visit is tagged attested; day defaulted to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from that file.
stops.campa: A Chilean diplomat and esotericist climbs the hill to the Casa Camuzzi and is received. Miguel Serrano has come from the far south of the world and finds an old man who tells him he has walked the same eastward road. The friendship runs by letter for eleven years. Serrano will carry it north to Küsnacht on Lake Zürich and the house of Carl Gustav Jung, arriving there, as Jung's own record has it, from Hermann Hesse's door, and will make of the two old men a matched pair of spiritual fathers.
suggested_refs: Miguel Serrano, C.G. Jung and Hermann Hesse: A Record of Two Friendships

stops.name: Montagnola, the Hermetic Circle
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in serrano.journey.json, with the quotation sourced there to Hermann Hesse speaking to Serrano at Montagnola on 22 January 1961.
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of January Serrano comes to lunch. Nothing happens by chance, the old man tells him: only the right guests meet here. Hesse is eighty-three. In June Jung dies at Küsnacht, and Serrano, left without either of his fathers of the spirit, starts the book that will bind the two of them together for readers who never met either man. Hesse has nineteen more months. He spends them as he has spent the last twenty years, answering letters from strangers who have read Demian and want to be told what to do.
stops.quote: nothing happens by chance ... here only the right guests meet, this is the Hermetic Circle
stops.quote_source: Hermann Hesse to Miguel Serrano, Montagnola, 22 January 1961, as preserved in A Record of Two Friendships and quoted in serrano.journey.json
suggested_refs: The Hermetic Circle, Hesse's phrase to Serrano at Montagnola

stops.name: Montagnola, the death
stops.date_confidence: 9 August 1962 per hermann-hesse.de and both Wikipedias. The UCSB Hesse project timeline prints 1961, and serrano.journey.json states that Hesse followed Jung into the ground within two months of June 1961, which is wrong by fourteen months. Both errors are recorded here rather than silently corrected elsewhere.
stops.campa: He dies at Montagnola on the ninth of August, eighty-five years old, of a cerebral hemorrhage. He has lived forty-three years on this hill, longer than he ever lived in Germany, and he has outlived the empire he was born under, the war he refused to bless, the republic that followed it, and the Reich that drove his friends past his door into exile. The obituaries call him the last of the German romantics. He has not carried a German passport since 1923, and he asked for the Swiss one himself.
suggested_refs: The Casa Rossa, Montagnola, where Hesse died on 9 August 1962

stops.name: Gentilino, the grave at Sant'Abbondio
stops.date_confidence: burial two days after the death is attested. Coordinate corrected to the Cimitero di Sant'Abbondio (Nominatim, Risciana, Gentilino); the pool carried two different points for this one graveyard, 45.9908, 8.9436 and 45.9989, 8.9346, both wrong by more than a kilometre. The claim that the cemetery was inaugurated in 1843 is unsupported and dropped.
stops.campa: Two days later he is buried at Sant'Abbondio in Gentilino, a walk down the hill, in a neoclassical churchyard on a terrace above the lake. The stone is plain enough that visitors walk past it looking for it. Hugo Ball has lain here since 1927 and Emmy Ball-Hennings beside him; so does the conductor Bruno Walter, who fled Germany as Hesse's friends fled it. Ninon will join him in 1966. The enclosure on the Ticinese hillside holds a good part of the German emigration of one century.
suggested_refs: The Cimitero di Sant'Abbondio, Gentilino, Collina d'Oro

stops.name: Los Angeles, a band takes the name Steppenwolf
stops.date_confidence: late 1967 per en.wikipedia, 'Steppenwolf (band)'; the 1968 date in circulation is wrong, as is the description of the Sparrows as a Los Angeles band. Day unknown, defaulted to 01. The Leary attribution is second-hand, reported by the New Statesman in 2018.
stops.campa: A Toronto band called the Sparrows, reformed in Los Angeles, is renamed on the suggestion of their producer Gabriel Mekler, who has read a German novel of 1927 about a man split between a citizen and a beast. In August 1968 Steppenwolf take Born to Be Wild to number two on the Billboard chart and put the words heavy metal into a rock lyric for the first time. Timothy Leary has already told his followers to read Siddhartha and Der Steppenwolf before dosing. Hesse, who drank wine, smoked, and had no interest in drugs, has been dead six years.

stops.name: Montagnola, Serrano in Hesse's own house

The 1997 museum opening is attested by de.wikipedia, 'Montagnola'; its own coordinate, 45.98297, 8.91884, differs from the inherited Montagnola pin used here.
stops.campa: Miguel Serrano, stripped of his ambassadorship, comes back to the Collina d'Oro and takes rooms in the Casa Camuzzi, the house where Hesse lived and wrote for twenty years and up to which he first climbed as a pilgrim in 1951. The visitor becomes the tenant of the address. In 1997 the neighbouring Torre Camuzzi opens as the Museo Hermann Hesse: the glasses, the typewriter, and the watercolours set behind glass in the rooms where the painting started in the summer of 1919.

stops.name: Calw, the museum on the Marktplatz
stops.date_confidence: March 1990 attested for the opening in the Haus Schüz; day unknown, defaulted to 01. The United States paperback figure of some 30 million is the reporting outlet's own estimate and is rendered here as tens of millions.
stops.campa: In March a museum opens in the Haus Schüz on the Marktplatz at Calw, a few doors from the room where he was born, holding manuscripts, first editions, personal effects, and the watercolours. The Württemberg town that produced a Protestant seminary boy and then broke him now lives partly on his name. In the United States the paperbacks of Siddhartha, Demian, and Steppenwolf have sold in the tens of millions since the 1960s. The boy who left school at fifteen with a one-year certificate is a set text.
